meta.audience: The people of Limhi, then Limhi and Ammon in private

world_behind.title: A second expedition, also lost
world_behind.text: Forty-three men sent to find Zarahemla wander many days, fail, and come home. The chapter before had sixteen men lost for forty days. Two search parties in two chapters, both diligent and both unsuccessful, and the second failure is what produces the discovery.

world_behind.title: Limhi's own plates, read aloud
world_behind.text: Verse 5 has the colony's record brought out for Ammon to read. It had been kept since they left Zarahemla two generations before. That document is where the next fourteen chapters come from. The reader is watching the compiler's source arrive in the narrative, handed across by a king who cannot read the other set of plates on his table.

world_behind.title: An older word for the same office
world_behind.text: First Samuel pauses its own narrative to explain that "seer" is what a prophet used to be called, a gloss for readers to whom the term had gone archaic. Both words are live in this colony, and neither Limhi nor Ammon treats either as obsolete.

world_behind.title: A restricted instrument
world_behind.text: Verse 13 says no man may look in the interpreters unless commanded, "lest he should look for that he ought not and he should perish." The danger attaches to unauthorized use. Israelite law usually guards sacred objects that way.

world_behind.title: Wisdom, personified and refused
world_behind.text: Verse 20 says they will not seek wisdom, "neither do they desire that she should rule over them." The pronoun is Proverbs': wisdom as a woman who calls in the street (Prov. 1:20) and is ignored. Limhi's lament is built on that figure.

world_behind.title: The scattered flock
world_behind.text: Verse 21's wild flock fleeing the shepherd, scattered, driven, devoured by beasts, is Ezekiel's picture of a people without a shepherd (Ezek. 34:5) and the one the gospels use of a crowd (Matt. 9:36). Limhi applies it to his own nation, in chains, at the end of a speech about refusing wisdom.

words.text: To recount in order, not to practice. Treated at 1 Nephi 15:20. Ammon rehearses the history of both peoples and then rehearses Benjamin's last words and explains them. The word marks the transfer of two records by speech, before any plates change hands, and it is likely what a people cut off for two generations most needed.

Armor, though the King James Bible mostly uses the word for the high priest's ornamented vestment in Exodus. Limhi's are plain equipment, "large, and they are of brass and of copper" (v. 10), and they come off the field of bones the lost expedition stumbled into. Ether 15:15 will describe that nation gathering for its last battle armed with shields and breastplates, women and children included. The gear reaches the reader before the war it was worn in does.

cites.quote: large, and they are of brass and of copper

spans.text: large, and they are of brass and of copper

words.text: Named as a thing rather than described: "the things are called interpreters." Ammon supplies the term as though it will be unfamiliar, and the record will use it five more times. The noun is functional: they interpret, and the man commanded to use them is given a different title.

The only occurrence in scripture. Ammon produces it in the middle of ranking the offices, and what the word does there is additive: the higher title absorbs the lower. Nothing is subtracted by being called the greater thing.

Not a puzzle without an answer. In scripture a mystery is a thing hidden that is meant to be opened, which is why unfolding is the verb Limhi reaches for. He uses the singular for what is written on the twenty-four plates, then the plural a beat later for whatever else the interpreters were prepared to open. The plural is the record's usual form. The singular narrows the word to one object, and that object is a document nobody in the land can read.

Not to be pierced or entered. Limhi applies it to understandings, paired with blind. The failure it names is structural. The word appears once in scripture and it is doing the work of explaining why a nation with a warning still ended in chains.

phrases.term: Only a few of them have I written in this book
phrases.text: Mormon interrupting his own narrative to say what he left out. The notice comes in the middle of a sentence about Limhi speaking, and it is the compiler reminding the reader once again that what survives is a selection made by one man.

phrases.term: Rehearsed unto them the last words which king Benjamin had taught them, and explained them
phrases.text: A sermon delivered secondhand to a people who were not there, with commentary. The address of Mosiah 2 through 5 crosses to a second nation by memory and explanation before it crosses on plates. It is the record's clearest picture of how teaching actually traveled.

phrases.term: Having discovered a land which was covered with bones of men, and of beasts
phrases.text: The report of the failed expedition, and the failure is what makes it valuable. They did not find Zarahemla; they found a graveyard the size of a nation. The sentence keeps piling clauses (many waters, bones, ruins, a people as numerous as the hosts of Israel) without pausing to react.

phrases.term: Twenty-four plates which are filled with engravings, and they are of pure gold
phrases.text: Brought back "for a testimony that the things that they had said are true." The plates are produced as evidence for a travel report before anyone knows what is on them. Their contents will occupy an entire book of this record, and here they are an exhibit.

phrases.term: The hilts thereof have perished, and the blades thereof were cankered with rust
phrases.text: Organic material gone, metal corroded, and in the same inventory the breastplates are "perfectly sound" and the gold plates are legible. The differential decay is exactly right, and it is reported by a king with no interest in the metals at all, only in the fact that nobody can read the writing.

phrases.term: I am desirous to know the cause of their destruction
phrases.text: The question that motivates the whole request, and it is not antiquarian. Limhi is in bondage and wants to know why a civilization died. The book of Ether exists in the record because a king in chains asked a practical question about a ruin.

phrases.term: He has wherewith that he can look, and translate all records that are of ancient date
phrases.text: Deliberately vague about the mechanism and precise about the result. "Wherewith that he can look" names an instrument without describing it. Ammon has just told Limhi he cannot interpret languages himself, so what he is offering is access to one. The same verse fences the instrument: "no man can look in them except he be commanded... lest he should look for that he ought not" (v. 13). The danger is defined as looking for the wrong thing, the restriction lands on the seeker's intent, and the stated penalty is perishing. It is the record's only rule about the use of a sacred instrument.

cites.quote: no man can look in them except he be commanded... lest he should look for that he ought not

spans.text: no man can look in them except he be commanded
lest he should look for that he ought not

phrases.term: A seer is greater than a prophet
phrases.text: Limhi's conclusion, and Ammon does not simply confirm it. The reply in verse 16 makes the seer a revelator and a prophet also, which converts a comparison into an accumulation. The exchange is the record's only discussion of how the offices relate.

phrases.term: Hidden things shall come to light, and things which are not known shall be made known
phrases.text: Four clauses saying nearly the same thing, escalating: secret things manifest, hidden things to light, unknown things made known, and things that could not otherwise be known. The last clause is the only one that adds anything, and it is what the whole verse exists for.

phrases.term: He becometh a great benefit to his fellow beings
phrases.text: The point of the gift, stated flatly at the end of a passage about power. Not that the seer is exalted or vindicated but that he is useful. Benjamin's argument about service and Ammon's about seership land in the same place.

phrases.term: They will not seek wisdom, neither do they desire that she should rule over them
phrases.text: Wisdom as a person who might govern, and a people who decline. The verb is desire rather than obey. The refusal happens before any command is issued. Limhi has just watched his own nation demonstrate this, and the sentence reads as grief.

phrases.term: As a wild flock which fleeth from the shepherd, and scattereth
phrases.text: Four verbs and every one of them passive after the first: flee, scatter, be driven, be devoured. The only choice in the sequence is the first, and everything after it happens to them. It is the last sentence of Limhi's speech and it describes what has already occurred.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: An omission conceded inside the first sentence
verses.text: The chapter's opening clause is interrupted by the abridger accounting for himself: "after king Limhi had made an end of speaking to his people, for he spake many things unto them and only a few of them have I written in this book, he caused that his people should assemble." The aside is grammatically unnecessary and sits between the subject and its verb. A speech is reported as having happened, its length is acknowledged, and its absence from the page is admitted, all before the sentence completes.

verses.label: v. 2–3
verses.title: Two long retellings, reported and not given
verses.text: Ammon performs two summaries and neither is reproduced. He rehearses "all that had happened unto their brethren from the time that Zeniff went up out of the land even until the time that he himself came up out of the land," and he rehearses "the last words which king Benjamin had taught them, and explained them to the people of king Limhi." A reader already has Benjamin's words at Mosiah 2 through 5, and will be given Zeniff's account at Mosiah 9. The record notes that both were delivered aloud here and declines to print either.

verses.label: v. 6
verses.title: A man's inability preserved on the record
verses.text: The question and the answer both survive: "the king inquired of him to know if he could interpret languages, and Ammon told him that he could not." Nothing depends on the exchange except the next seven verses, which are about finding someone who can. The chapter could have moved straight to the recommendation. Instead it keeps the moment where the visiting hero says no.

verses.label: v. 8–11
verses.title: Three artefacts, described by their condition
verses.text: The inventory is unusually physical and notes what has survived and what has not. Twenty-four plates "filled with engravings, and they are of pure gold." Breastplates "which are large, and they are of brass and of copper, and are perfectly sound." Swords whose "hilts thereof have perished, and the blades thereof were cankered with rust." Gold and copper alloy are reported intact and iron is reported gone, which is what a buried assemblage of those materials would look like. The record does not draw attention to the contrast; it simply lists each object with its state.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: A translation requested for a stated and uncertain reason
verses.text: The king's purpose is given with a hedge in the middle of it: "I am desirous that these records should be translated into our language; for, perhaps, they will give us a knowledge of a remnant of the people who have been destroyed." Perhaps is doing real work. He wants the documents read without knowing what is in them, and the possibility he names, information about a vanished people, is exactly what the record turns out to contain in the book of Ether.

verses.label: v. 13–18
verses.title: A definition attempted three times in three verses
verses.text: The exchange builds the word by comparison instead of by statement. Verse 15: "a seer is greater than a prophet." Verse 16: "a seer is a revelator and a prophet also." Verse 17: "a seer can know of things which are past, and also of things which are to come." Inside verse 17 the speaker corrects himself mid-clause: "by them shall all things be revealed, or, rather, shall secret things be made manifest." The record keeps the first formulation alongside the revision instead of printing only the better one.

verses.label: v. 19–21
verses.title: The response quoted, ending on a flock
verses.text: The king's reaction runs three verses and is given as speech: "Doubtless a great mystery is contained within these plates." What follows is not about the plates at all but about people, "how blind and impenetrable are the understandings of the children of men; for they will not seek wisdom, neither do they desire that she should rule over them." Then a simile closes it: "they are as a wild flock which fleeth from the shepherd, and scattereth, and are driven, and are devoured by the beasts of the forest." A chapter about documents ends on an image with no document in it.

chapter.title: A failure produces the most valuable thing in the chapter
chapter.text: Forty-three men set out to find Zarahemla and did not. What they brought back instead was a dead nation's record, and the book that comes out of it closes the whole volume. The record does not treat this as irony; it simply reports the sequence.

chapter.title: The offices are ranked, against the Hebrew Bible's grain
chapter.text: 1 Samuel 9:9 makes the two words equivalent across time, "he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer." Verse 15 here states a ranking instead, "a seer is greater than a prophet," and verse 16 answers by addition rather than subtraction, "a seer is a revelator and a prophet also." Verse 17 then supplies the working definition in four clauses, past things, things to come, secret things made manifest, and hidden things brought to light. The exchange is a definition being negotiated between two speakers in four verses.

chapter.title: The gift is defined by what it produces for other people
chapter.text: Verse 18 ends the discussion on benefit to one's fellow beings. After four verses about extraordinary capacity, the summary is that the man is useful, the same move Benjamin made about kingship.

chapter.title: A king in bondage asks a research question
chapter.text: Limhi wants the plates translated to learn why that civilization was destroyed. He does not sound curious; he is a ruler whose own people are being crushed, looking for a case study. The book of Ether enters the record as an answer to a practical question.

chapter.title: Benjamin's address travels by memory before it travels by plates
chapter.text: Ammon rehearses it and explains it to a nation that was not there. The most important sermon in the record reaches its second audience through one man's recollection, and the chapter notes that he had to explain it as well as repeat it.

chapter.title: The chapter ends on refusal rather than on discovery
chapter.text: After plates, interpreters, and seers, Limhi's last words are about people who will not seek wisdom or let her govern them, and a flock devoured because it fled. The instruments exist; the obstacle named is that nobody wants what they offer.

applications.title: Bring back what you found
applications.text: The expedition failed and reported anyway. When something does not work out, take inventory of what you did encounter before writing the attempt off.

applications.title: Ask the practical question about a ruin
applications.text: Limhi asked for the cause of a destruction while his own people sat in bondage (v. 7). Study a failure, whether a family's, an institution's, or your own, with the question "why did this end" rather than "wasn't that sad."

applications.title: Rehearse and explain
applications.text: Ammon did both. When you pass on something you were taught, repeat it accurately and then say what it means, because the second audience was not in the room.

applications.title: Measure a gift by its benefit
applications.text: The chapter's summary of extraordinary spiritual capacity is that the man becomes useful. Take whatever you are good at and ask who is actually better off.

applications.title: Notice what you decline before it is offered
applications.text: The refusal in the verse happens at the level of desire. Ask what you have quietly decided you would rather not have govern you.

applications.title: Watch the first verb
applications.text: Flee, scatter, be driven, be devoured. Only the first was a choice. Identify a drift in your life and find the one voluntary step at the front of it.

questions.text: What did I find while failing at something else, and did I bother to report it?
Whose collapse could teach me something if I looked at it honestly?
Have I ever wanted access to something sacred for a reason I would not want examined?
Do I care more about the rank of a calling than about what it does?
Who is better off because of the thing I am best at?
What would it cost me to let wisdom actually rule, rather than advise?
